title: Danville City Councilman Seriously Injured in Gasoline Attack; Community Grapples with Public Safety Concerns
text:
Danville City Councilman J.
Lee Vogler, 38, was left in critical condition after being doused in gasoline and set alight in his office by a man who police have identified as Shotsie Michael Buck Hayes, 29.
Vogler is happily married to wife Blair, the mother of his children, and recently shared a gushing birthday tribute to her on Facebook The alleged attack, which occurred at Showcase Magazine HQ around 11:30 a.m. on Wednesday, has sent shockwaves through the community and raised urgent questions about the intersection of personal conflict and public safety.
According to Andrew Brooks, the owner of Showcase Magazine, Hayes stormed into the office, poured the contents of a five-gallon container onto Vogler, and then ignited the liquid, leaving the councilman with severe burns.
Brooks, who later shared a tearful video recounting the incident, described Vogler as ‘awake and talking’ after being airlifted to Central Lynchburg General Hospital for treatment.
Danville City Councilman J. Lee Vogler, 38, was airlifted to a regional burn center after being set on fire inside his office Wednesday morning However, police have not yet released detailed information about the extent of Vogler’s injuries, citing the ongoing investigation.
The attack, which authorities have labeled a ‘personal matter,’ is not believed to be related to Vogler’s role as a public official.
Instead, police have confirmed that Hayes and Vogler know each other, though the nature of their relationship and the specifics of their alleged dispute remain undisclosed.
The incident has drawn attention to the broader issue of how private conflicts can escalate into acts of violence, particularly in spaces where public figures are vulnerable.
Police said Shotsie Michael Buck Hayes (right), 29, of Danville carried out the attack on Wednesday Local experts in criminal justice have emphasized the need for communities to remain vigilant and report suspicious behavior, even in cases where the perpetrators are known to victims. ‘These situations often begin with personal disagreements, but they can quickly spiral into something far more dangerous,’ said Dr.
Emily Carter, a psychologist specializing in domestic violence at the University of Virginia. ‘It’s crucial for individuals in crisis to seek help before tensions reach this level.’
Adding to the complexity of the case is the recent divorce filing by Hayes’ wife, Mary Alice Buck-Hayes, who reportedly married her husband in 2021.
Vogler (right), who shares two young children with his wife, Blair Vogler (left), was the target of the alleged attack The couple’s separation, which was announced just two weeks prior to the attack, has prompted speculation about whether personal turmoil may have played a role in Hayes’ actions.
However, investigators have not yet commented on whether Hayes’ mental health or the divorce contributed to the violence. ‘We are in the early stages of this investigation, and we are not at liberty to share details about the suspect’s mental state,’ said Danville Police Department spokesperson Sarah Mitchell. ‘Our focus remains on ensuring the victim receives the care he needs and bringing the perpetrator to justice.’
Vogler, a native of Danville, has long been a prominent figure in local politics.
A tragic tale of infidelity and violence He made history in 2012 when he was elected to the City Council at the age of 24, becoming the youngest person ever to hold the position.
A graduate of Virginia Commonwealth University with a Bachelor’s degree in Political Science, Vogler has since served as Managing Partner at Andrew Brooks Media Group, the parent company of Showcase Magazine.
His personal life has also been a source of public admiration, particularly after he recently shared a heartfelt birthday tribute to his wife, Blair Vogler, on Facebook. ‘The kids and I are so blessed to have you in our lives,’ he wrote, highlighting the couple’s two young children.
The attack has left the community reeling, with many expressing concern for Vogler’s recovery and the well-being of his family.
As the investigation continues, police have urged the public to avoid speculation about Hayes’ motives and instead focus on the broader implications of the incident. ‘This type of senseless act of violence has to stop,’ Brooks said in his video, echoing sentiments shared by local leaders. ‘You do not have the right as a human being to get upset with someone enough to lash out and attempt to harm them in any way—much less this way.’ With Hayes currently held in Danville City Jail without bond, the case has become a focal point for discussions about mental health resources, domestic conflict resolution, and the need for stronger measures to prevent such tragedies.
For now, the community waits for answers, while Vogler’s family and friends remain at his side, hoping for a full recovery.
